texts.preamble: The Scotch Whisky Association vs Unibev Limited on 1 February, 2021 Author: Jayant Nath Bench: Jayant Nath $~Os-3 * In The High Court Of Delhi At New Delhi + Cs(Comm) 28/2021 The Scotch Whisky Association .... Plaintiff Through Mr.Sanjeev Sindhwani, Sr. Adv. with Mr.Prashant Gupta, Mr.Deepak Gogia, Mr.Jitin M. George and Mr.Sachin, Advs. versus Unibev Limited ..... Defendant Through Mr.Parag P.Tripathi, Sr.Adv. with Mr.Shailen Bhatia, Ms.Nishtha Kaura and Mr.Lalltaksh Joshi, Advs. Coram:
texts.facts: For the reasons stated in the application, the same is allowed. 1. This application is filed under Order 39 Rules 1 and 2 CPC seeking the following reliefs: "a) an order of interim injunction to restrain the Defendant by itself and its officers, servants, agents and representatives from manufacturing, bottling, selling, offering for sale, marketing, advertising, supplying, distributing, importing, exporting, stocking and dealing in, directly or indirectly, in any way whatsoever, in India or abroad, any whisky which is not Scotch Whisky under the mark "STROTTS" or by using any other mark, image, statement, expression or description which is indicative, suggestive or evocative of the United Kingdom or Scotch Whisky or which alludes or suggests a nexus or association with the United Kingdom or Scotch Whisky, or from committing or doing any other act so as to infringe the Plaintiff's registered geographical indication "SCOTCH WHISKY"; b) an order of interim injunction to restrain the Defendant by itself and its officers, servants, agents and representatives from manufacturing, bottling, selling, offering The Scotch Whisky Association vs Unibev Limited on 1 February, 2021 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/72539493/ 1 for sale, marketing, advertising, supplying, distributing, importing, exporting, stocking and dealing in, directly or indirectly, in any way whatsoever, in India or abroad, any whisky which is not Scotch Whisky under the description 'Scotch Whisky' or 'Blended Scotch Whisky', "Product of Scotland" or "Blended with X Year Old SCOTCH" or by using any other mark, image, statement, expression or description which is indicative, suggestive or evocative of the United Kingdom or Scotch Whisky or which alludes or suggests a nexus or association with the United Kingdom or Scotch Whisky, or from committing or doing any other act so as to infringe the Plaintiff's registered geographical indication "SCOTCH WHISKY"; and c) an order of interim injunction to restrain the Defendant by itself and its officers, servants, agents and representatives from manufacturing, bottling, selling, offering for sale, marketing, advertising, supplying, distributing, importing, exporting, stocking and dealing in, directly or indirectly, in any way whatsoever, in India or abroad, from using upon or in relation to its business and products, expressions such as "Blended with upto X Year Old Scotch and Matured Indian Malts" or any other statement, expression or description which falsely convey the maturation age of the spirit, and in particular, from using numbers to convey the age of the spirit unless such number pertains to the youngest component in the spirit." 2. It is the case of the plaintiff that it is incorporated with the object of protecting and promoting the interests of Scotch whisky trade and represents the collective interest of Scotch whisky industry. 3. It is stated that Scotch whisky is a world-renowned Geographical Indication originating from Scotland, UK which refers to whisky produce exclusively in Scotland. The said Scotch whisky is registered under No.151 in class 33 of the Geographical Indication of Goods (Registration & Protection) Act, 1999 (herein after refers to as the 'GI Act'). Further as per Notification w.e.f. 28.11.2011 Scotch whisky has been afforded additional protection.
texts.arguments: 4. It is pleaded that in view of the statutory and common law rights of the plaintiff in the GI (Scotch Whiskey), any whisky which is not Scotch whisky, if sold or advertised bearing an expression or description or get-up or reference or indication to Scottish origin, is likely to mislead members of the trade and the public all over the world including India into believing that such whisky is Scotch whisky. Any such act would violate the plaintiff's statutory and common law rights in the GI "Scotch Whisky". 5. It is further stated that several whisky producers around the world including manufacturers of Scotch whisky, permanently use numerals on the front label of their labelling and packaging to highlight the age statement (a reference to the period of maturation) of their whiskies. It is common knowledge that a whisky with higher age statement commands a higher price as compared to the whisky of a lower age statement. The use of false and misleading age statements on whiskies violates the Scotch Whisky Regulation, 2009 and is an act of unfair competition amounting to infringement under Section 22 (1)(b) of the GI Act. Reliance is also placed on Rule 1.3.7 of the Food Safety & Standards (Alcoholic Beverages) Regulations, 2018 (FSSAI Regulations) which mandates that the The Scotch Whisky Association vs Unibev Limited on 1 February, 2021 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/72539493/ 2 age of spirit whisky must refer to the youngest spirit. Hence it is pleaded that both the FSSAI Regulations and the EU Spirit Drinks Regulation mean that if a bottle of whisky shows an age statement of 12 years old, it implies that the youngest whisky in the bottle is at least 12 years old. These Regulations recognize the real threat that if consumers see an age statement on the labelling of a whisky, then such consumer is likely to believe that all components of whisky are matured for the length of time as mentioned on the labelling. 6. Regarding the defendant, it is stated that it is engaged in the business of manufacturing, exporting and supplying of liquor products including whisky, rum, gin, beer etc. With the motive to benefit from the reputation and goodwill of Scotch whisky, the defendant is selling and advertising its whisky sold under the brands "STROTTS" as blended Scotch whisky and also using the phrase "Product of Scotland". However, in fact, the product is not registered with Her Majesty's Revenue and Customs in the United Kingdom, which is a mandatory requirement for procuring Scotch whisky in bulk. The defendant is committing an act of infringement of statutory rights of the plaintiff in the registered GI "Scotch whisky" within the meaning of Sections 22(1)(a) and (b) of GI Act. 7. It is further stated that the defendant is using untrue and misleading statements such as "Blended with upto 18 year old Scotch and Matured Indian Malts", "Blended with upto 15 year old Scotch and Matured Indian Malts", "Blended with upto 12 year old Scotch and Matured Indian Malts", "Blended with upto 21 year old Scotch and Matured Indian Malts", in relation to its whiskies sold under the brands OAKTON, GOVERNOR'S RESERVE Select Double Grain Whisky, GOVERNOR'S RESERVE 100% Premium Grain Whisky, ROYALTON, and SEVENTH HEAVEN. Evidently, these numerals do not refer to the youngest component of the whisky. Further, these numerals are depicted prominently and in a separate line on the defendant's packaging and label to create a false impression that the said numerals refer to the 'age' of the whiskies. Use of such false and misleading age statements by the defendant is a deliberate and calculated act to mislead the unwary customers into believing that the defendant's whiskies have been aged for 18/15/12/21 years, as the case may be. It is pleaded that considering that the consumers in India are well aware with the use of numerals on whisky to detonate the age of the whisky, the calculated positioning of numerals on the packaging of its whisky by the defendant is likely to deceive consumers into believing that it is an age statement. Such a statement amounts to false trade description within the meaning of Sections 2(1)(za) and 2(1)(i) of the Trademark Act. Further the age statements use the GI Scotch Whisky in a manner which is likely to mislead the general public as to the nature and characteristics of the product. As far as STROTTS whisky is concerned, he further states that he has instructions to state that it is 100% imported from Scotland and he will file due papers in this regard. The Scotch Whisky Association vs Unibev Limited on 1 February, 2021 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/72539493/ 3 9. As far as the "STROTTS WHISKY" is concerned, the learned counsel for the defendant has already stated that he has instructions to state that it is 100% imported from Scotland. The defendant will abide by the said statement and only such Scotch whisky, which is imported from Scotland and fulfils the requirements of being described as a Scotch whisky will be used by the defendant. Learned senior counsel for the plaintiff has urged as follows: i. He pleads that the above method of representing the age of the Scotch whisky is illegal and is barred by Section 22 of the GI Act. ii. He further states that under Section 92(2)(v) of the Food Safety & Standards Act, 2006 concerned Ministry has issued a notification dated 19.03.2018 whereby Food Safety & Standards (Alcoholic Beverages) Regulation 2018 were passed. These are similar to the Spirit and Drinks Regulation Rule 1.3.7 of SS Regulations which mandates that the age of spirit whisky must refer the youngest spirit in the blend. Hence, it is stated that under both the above regulations, if a bottle of Scotch whisky shows a statement e.g. 12 years old, it implies that the youngest Scotch whisky in the bottle is at least 12 years old. It is pleaded that the defendants are violating the said Regulation. iii. He also relies upon judgment of a Single Bench of the Bombay High Court in the case of The Scotch Whisky Association & Anr. vs. Pravara Sahakar Shakar Karkhana Ltd., AIR 1992 Bom 294 or 1991 SSC OnLine Bom 271. 13. Learned senior counsel for the defendant has pleaded as follows: i. He state that the FSSAI Act bars jurisdiction of a civil court. Hence, it is pleaded that in case the plaintiff seeks to rely upon such statutory provision, then this court would have no jurisdiction to decide the present suit. ii. He also relies upon the judgment of the Supreme Court in the case of Khoday Distilleries Ltd. vs. Scotch Whisky Association & Ors., (2008) 10 SCC 723 to urge that the judgment relied upon by the plaintiff in the case of The Scotch Whisky Association and other vs. Pravara Sahakar Shakar Karkhana Ltd. no longer is good law. iii. He further pleads that the plaintiff is unable to explain under what statutory provision the defendants are barred from representing the age of the blended Scotch The Scotch Whisky Association vs Unibev Limited on 1 February, 2021 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/72539493/ 4 whisky as being reflected on the labels by the defendants. 14. 15. I may look at the judgment of the Single Bench of the Bombay High Court in the case of The Scotch Whisky Association and other vs. Pravara Sahakar Shakar Karkhana Ltd.(supra). In those facts, the Bombay High Court held as follows: "5. It has been averred in paragraph 7 of the plaint that members of the 1st plaintiff, including the 2nd plaintiff, who distill scotch whisky and market it all over the world, use various well known brand names such as "Royal Salute", "Chivas Regal", "100 Pipes", "Red Label", "Johnnie Walker-Black Label" etc. or devices showing well known Scottish figures or Scottish soldiers or Scottish Headgears or Scottish emblems. The defendant however has been contending that the defendant is entitled to use the words "Blended With Scotch" on the label or on the carton as the said words do not and cannot convey misleading impression to the purchasers that the whisky marketed by the defendants is blended scotch whisky. It is the contention of the defendants that even if the defendants mix a small or negligible percentage of The Scotch Whisky Association vs Unibev Limited on 1 February, 2021 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/72539493/ 5 scotch whisky as an ingredient along with its Indian whiskies in the blend, the defendant would be justified in describing its product as a "whisky blended with scotch". Learned senior counsel for the defendant has however sought to rely upon the judgment of the Supreme Court in the case of Khoday Distilleries Ltd. vs. Scotch Whisky Association & Ors.(supra). It was also pleaded the word 'Peter Scot' allegedly being evolved from Scotland cannot be held to be a subject matter of passing off as purchasers of the same were discerning, they were aware of the brand which they would be purchasing and rich and wealthy people would only ordinarily purchase goods like scotch whisky and they being literate cannot possibly be pulled by the word 'Scot' knowing that they are purchasing scotch whisky. It was in those facts that the Supreme Court held as follows: "82.
